newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Romania's exiled king leaves Switzerland for home.
newsitem.headline: Romania's exiled king leaves Switzerland for home.

text.p: Exiled King Michael of Romania, who was given back his citizenship last week after 50 years, left Geneva on Thursday for a six-day visit to his homeland.
The last time he tried to visit, in 1995, he was bundled back on to a plane by the then leftist authorities there.

Michael, 75, a member of the German Hohenzollern dynasty, was forced to abdicate and go into exile in 1947 by Communists who seized power in Romania with Moscow's help after World War Two. He was stripped of his citizenship one year later.
"A whole lifetime's waiting has been rewarded today," the exiled king, who lives in Switzerland, said in a statement.
"I'm coming to help you leave the troubles of the past behind. I'm coming...to unite, not to divide," he said.

Michael, a shy, softspoken retired businessman, is revered by many Romanians for his courage as a young monarch during World War Two, when he arrested fascist leader Marshal Ion Antonescu and switched Romania to the Allied side.

During his first visit home in 1992, three years after the execution of communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, the former king was feted by hundreds of thousands of well-wishers who poured into Bucharest streets at Orthodox Easter.
Michael's later homecoming attempts had been blocked by Romania's former leftist authorities under ex-President Ion Iliescu, who lost office in an election last November.
The ex-communists treated Michael as a foreign commoner and linked his entry visa to his recognition of the constitution of 1991 which defines Romania as a semi-presidential republic.
But Romania's new reformist president, Emil Constantinescu, has said he plans to give a dinner in Michael's honour at his Cotroceni palace, a former royal residence.

Bucharest sees a new role for Michael in lobbying for support for its bid to join NATO, along with more developed fellow east Europeans Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, when the Alliance issues formal invitation to states to allow first eastward expansion at a Madrid summit in July.

Michael said he would not be engaged in any constitutional or property issues during his current visit, accompanied by his wife, Ana of Bourbon Parma, and his eldest daughter, Princess Margareta, who married a Romanian actor in Switzerland in 1996.
According to opinion polls, only a small fraction of Romanians favour restoration of the monarchy.
